newsitem.title: Austria: FOCUS-Vienna market cheers Austrian bank deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Vienna market cheers Austrian bank deal.

text.p: Vienna's stock market greeted Bank Austria's acquisition of Creditanstalt bank by jumping to a 33-month high on Monday, but Creditanstalt executives were left in the dark.
A day after Austria's biggest banking merger since World War Two secured the survival of the frayed government coalition, Creditanstalt said it had yet to hear of Bank Austria's plans.
"We still haven't heard from either Bank Austria or the government," a Creditanstalt spokesman said.
Bank Austria, having swallowed its main rival to create a financial powerhouse that will rank among Europe's top 30 banks, also kept a low profile.
In a brief statement, it merely asked Creditanstalt's non-executive supervisory board chief Walter Fremuth to stay on in his job following his offer to resign on Monday.

On the Vienna bourse there was a flurry of activity as investors scrambled to pick up shares of Creditanstalt, seen as the main gainer from the deal. Creditanstalt's preference stock jumped 3.7 percent, while its common shares rose 0.85 percent.
The ATX index of 21 blue chips jumped 26.12 points or 2.29 percent to 1,167.43.
"The political uncertainty has been removed, that's the main thing," said one trader.

Hopes that Creditanstalt may benefit from Bank Austria's triple-A credit rating -- ensured by the City of Vienna's guarantee for the bank's liabilities -- were nurtured when rating agency IBCA said it may upgrade Creditanstalt's present short and long-term ratings of A1 and A plus.

Bank Austria hailed the acquisition as the biggest step in its history, but analysts said it remained to be seen whether the new banking goliath could reap enough synergies to bring a quick return on the 17.2 billion schilling ($1.54 billion) investment.

Bank Austria was given the green light for the deal after an emergency session of government leaders, who drew up several pages of fine print to make sure the merger did not cause too much political fallout.
Bank Austria had to agree to keep Creditanstalt independent for at least five years and to extend a job guarantee to all of the bank's 9,800 employees.
Analysts said the delayed fusion would make it difficult to cut the fat quickly enough and said other details of the banks' future strategies also remained sketchy.
"There is a five year period where basically nothing will change. That takes the commercial logic out of the deal," said Gerhard Auer, Austria analyst at ICE Securities in London.
Bank Austria on Sunday predicted the deal would double shareholder value over the next five years and result in several billions of schillings in extra revenue.
But chief executive Gerhard Randa, seen as the key figure behind the deal, privately admitted that there would be "substantial" initial charges against current-year earnings.
The European Commission poured more cold water on the deal when a spokesman said it was investigating whether any public subsidies were involved.

In return for becoming the biggest force in modern-day Austrian business life, Bank Austria had to accept a gradual loss of public control over the next five years and the prospect of having to pay a fee in return for the City of Vienna's liability guarantee.

The new Alpine superbank will almost completely dominate the domestic scene. With total assets of some 1,400 billion schillings, it will control 80 percent of Vienna bourse trade, 70 percent of commercial banking and half of export financing. ($1=11.15 Schilling)
